Reading A construes it as uncreated divine speech, making revelation itself a permanent ontic constraint that grounds prophetic authority and benefits doctrinal literalism and juristic permanence; Reading B construes it as created, locating divine transcendence above the text and shifting constraint toward rational theology and state-backed doctrinal flexibility, with literalist communities and fixed-meaning claims among the principal victim sets.

human_readable: John 1:1 and the status of the Logos
summary: KERNEL CONTEST: [ANALYTICAL ESTIMATE] The fixed substrate is John 1:1 and its opening Logos formulation. Reading A treats the Logos as preexistent and divine, generating a constraint profile centered on incarnation, sacramental authority, and Christological continuity; Reading B reads the passage as poetic or functional language about divine wisdom or plan, moving constraint toward non-incarnational monotheism and diminished doctrinal exclusivity, with high-church sacramental systems and strong incarnation claims as the main victim set.

human_readable: Deuteronomy 7 and the ban of herem
summary: KERNEL CONTEST: [ANALYTICAL ESTIMATE] The fixed substrate is Deuteronomy 7’s command to destroy or expel certain peoples and refuse covenantal mixing. Reading A treats the passage as a durable divine command that structures identity through separation, obedience, and bounded membership; Reading B reads it as historically situated, allegorical, or morally superseded, shifting constraint toward universal ethics and limiting ethnoreligious exclusion, while conquest ideologies and purity-bound communities become the primary beneficiaries under Reading A and the primary victims under Reading B.

human_readable: Magna Carta and the limits of sovereignty
summary: KERNEL CONTEST: [ANALYTICAL ESTIMATE] The fixed substrate is Magna Carta of 1215 as a stabilized charter text. Reading A treats it as a living source of due process, lawful restraint, and inherited liberties that binds rulers and benefits subjects against arbitrary power; Reading B treats it as a feudal bargain of its time with narrow baronial scope, shifting constraint toward absolute sovereignty and executive discretion, with popular constitutionalism as the victim set in the latter reading and royal prerogative as the victim set in the former.

human_readable: The Second Amendment and the militia clause
summary: KERNEL CONTEST: [ANALYTICAL ESTIMATE] The fixed substrate is the Second Amendment’s text on a well regulated militia and the right to keep and bear arms. Reading A treats the militia clause as a collective-security frame that conditions arms on civic defense, emphasizing state regulation and public-order beneficiaries; Reading B treats the same text as an individual-right guarantee detached from militia service, producing a constraint profile centered on personal armament and strong resistance to regulation, with state police power and disarmed-risk populations as key victims under Reading B.

human_readable: The Fourteenth Amendment and equal protection
summary: KERNEL CONTEST: [ANALYTICAL ESTIMATE] The fixed substrate is the Fourteenth Amendment’s Equal Protection and Due Process language. Reading A interprets it as a robust anti-caste rule requiring active state correction of racial, gender, or status hierarchy, benefiting subordinated groups and constraining entrenched privilege; Reading B interprets it as a narrow formal-equality principle limiting only explicit state discrimination, benefiting colorblind or minimalist state theories and leaving structural inequality largely intact, with remedial redistribution and affirmative enforcement as the chief victim set.

human_readable: Geneva Conventions and the meaning of lawful combat
summary: KERNEL CONTEST: [ANALYTICAL ESTIMATE] The fixed substrate is the 1949 Geneva Conventions and their rules on protected persons, prisoners of war, and civilians. Reading A treats the conventions as a hard humanitarian ceiling that limits force, expands protections, and burdens militaries regardless of reciprocity; Reading B treats them as reciprocal or conditional restraints that can be suspended against irregular enemies or degraded states, shifting constraint toward security maximization and making civilian immunity and detained-person protections the major victim set.

human_readable: IETF open standards and internet governance

Reading A treats openness, rough consensus, and interoperable standards as the governing constraint that preserves a public internet for users and implementers; Reading B treats standards as a substrate for control, enclosure, or platform capture, shifting constraint toward proprietary gatekeeping and monetized chokepoints, with open interoperability advocates and smaller implementers as the main victims under the latter reading.

KERNEL CONTEST: The biblical covenant between God and Abraham in Genesis serves as the fixed substrate. KERNEL CONTEST: The 1648 Peace of Westphalia establishing state sovereignty serves as the fixed substrate. Reading A (absolute sovereignty interpretation) views this as creating constraints against external interference in domestic affairs, benefiting state autonomy while potentially enabling human rights violations within borders. Reading B (responsibility to protect interpretation) sees sovereignty as conditional, creating constraints on state actions when human rights are threatened, benefiting international intervention advocates while potentially undermining state autonomy.

KERNEL CONTEST: The Geneva Conventions on wartime conduct serve as the fixed substrate. Reading B (universal human rights interpretation) extends protections to all combatants, creating constraints on state military actions that benefit non-state actors while potentially reducing state military effectiveness.

KERNEL CONTEST: The Takings Clause ('nor shall private property be taken for public use, without just compensation') serves as the fixed substrate. Reading B (broad interpretation) constrains regulations that substantially diminish property value, benefiting property owners with expanded protections while potentially limiting government regulatory power for public welfare.

KERNEL CONTEST: The 1944 Bretton Woods agreement establishing the dollar-gold standard serves as the fixed substrate.
